children.text: The video as a whole can be seen as a mild but clear example of ragebait. Joey does not generate controversy himself. He chooses an already divisive video and profits off of it. This is a much safer way to use ragebait to farm engagement. Many ragebait creators receive a lot of hate, and this does not lead to a loyal fanbase. By instead commenting on ragebait, Joey is able to build his own fanbase. By the time Joey actually enters the video after 35 seconds, he is mostly restating the ideas that the audience already formed. Rather than offering fresh insight, he uses sarcasm to provide the general consensus.

The beginning of the video lays the groundwork for the rest of the video. The video that Joey is commenting on plays almost in its entirety, so that the audience has context. By starting with this and not his own commentary, Joey allows the viewer to build their own opinion first. Since their opinion most likely aligns with what he is about to say, it builds his credibility. The video depicts a man in the gym doing curls. He is then approached and asked how many sets he has left. This method of giving the viewer context only works due to one of TikTok’s affordances, the stitch feature. He is able to directly attach his commentary to the video.

When Joey appears in the video, he is in his car. He is not in the gym or a branded set. This gives the video a feeling of immediately needing to be recorded. He did not wait to get home, instead he recorded the video right where he was. This better frames his commentary as authentic rather than being actually produced. The viewer is better able to see Joey as a relatable person rather than a big-time creator. After gaining this trust, viewers give more weight to the rest of the video since audiences tend to trust real people rather than manufactured content creators.
